title: Fewest Passes of a Run Printer
statement:
A printer works on a strip of paper. In one pass it picks one letter and a contiguous range of positions, and writes that letter on every position in the range, covering whatever was there before.

The strip starts blank. Return the fewest passes needed to make it read exactly s.

examples.why: Write a over all six positions, then b over the middle two. Counting letter runs would say 3.
Write a over positions 0–2, then b at 1 and b at 3. One b pass over 1–3 would destroy the a at position 2.
Three different letters always need three passes.

hints: Think about the first letter, s[0]. Some pass writes it. Which other positions could that same pass also finish?
If the pass that writes s[0] stretches to a later position k with the same letter, then the part between them is printed on top afterwards, independently of the rest.
Let f(i, j) be the answer for s[i..j]. Either s[i] gets its own pass, 1 + f(i+1, j), or it shares a pass with some s[k] == s[i]: f(i+1, k−1) + f(k, j).

explain.intuition:
Later passes cover earlier ones, so a long early pass works like a background. The question is which positions share a pass. Look at the leftmost position i. Either its pass prints nothing else that survives, costing 1 + f(i+1, j), or its pass also leaves the final letter at some later position k with s[k] == s[i].

In the second case the stretch between i and k is printed on top of the background, separately: f(i+1, k−1). And position k starts a subproblem f(k, j) whose first pass is that same shared pass, so it is not counted twice. Each state is a range (i, j), which makes this interval DP.
steps: Optionally collapse runs of equal letters first: "aabb" needs as many passes as "ab".
Define f(i, j) = fewest passes for s[i..j], with f(i, i) = 1 and an empty range costing 0.
For every k in i+1..j with s[k] == s[i], try f(i+1, k−1) + f(k, j) and keep the minimum.
Fill ranges from short to long (or memoise), and return f(0, n−1).
pitfalls: Counting runs of equal letters. "aabbaa" has three runs but needs two passes, because the a's share one background pass.
Adding 1 for the shared pass in both halves. The pass is paid for once, inside f(k, j).
Greedily joining s[i] with the farthest matching letter. Which k is best depends on what lies in between, so try them all.

solutions.title: Memoised recursion on the first letter
solutions.idea: The first letter either gets its own pass or shares one with a later equal letter k; memoise on the range.

solutions.title: Bottom-up table on the last letter
solutions.idea: Collapse equal neighbours, then fill dp[i][j] by length. The last letter either gets a new pass or extends the pass of an earlier equal letter k.

followups: Return the actual sequence of passes, not just how many.
Each pass may now only write over blank positions. How does the problem change?
